title: Bhuridatta's precepts
hook: a serpent prince keeps his precepts toward the man who caged him. should he?
tomorrow: what changes when you keep eight precepts for a day instead of five?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sila: five training rules taken up in the first person, good conduct kept as a gift to strangers. Today a gift to someone who doesn't deserve one.

Promises are easy to keep with people who are kind to you. So would you keep your word to the man who had caged you? In one of the long Jataka tales, a prince does exactly that, and the person he keeps it toward is the one holding the cage. Not everyone in the Buddhist world reads a precept as holding quite that far. Today, both sides get to speak.
screen: `EASY WITH KIND PEOPLE.` → `A PRINCE IN A CAGE.` → `HOW FAR DOES A PRECEPT HOLD?`

segments.voice: Bhuridatta is a naga prince, a serpent being with great power. He wants to keep the precepts on observance days, so he lies coiled on an anthill in the human world. A snake charmer finds him and, with a spell, seizes him. The story says Bhuridatta could have burned the man to ash in an instant. He doesn't. He keeps his eyes shut so his anger won't get out, and keeps his precepts. He's beaten, stuffed into a basket and made to dance for crowds, until his family finds him and he's set free. Kept under pressure. First view: this is the precept working. A precept with exceptions stops being a promise of safety, because every angry person can find an exception. Bhuridatta's restraint protects even the man who wronged him. Second view, from a Mahayana sutra on skill in means: a ship's captain, the Buddha in a past life, learns that one man aboard plans to murder all the merchants on the ship. Out of compassion, for the merchants and for the would-be killer, he kills him first, ready to bear the karmic cost himself. Here the rule serves compassion, not the other way round. Both texts take the precepts seriously. They differ on what to do when keeping one costs someone else's life.
screen: `A NAGA PRINCE ON AN ANTHILL.` · `HE SHUTS HIS EYES, AND KEEPS IT.` · `VIEW ONE: NO EXCEPTIONS.` · `VIEW TWO: THE CAPTAIN'S CHOICE.` · then, large: `KEPT UNDER PRESSURE.`

segments.voice: Choose one precept and picture the moment this week it'll be hardest to keep: the small lie that would smooth things over, the snap at someone who pushed you. Stand or sit tall, the way Bhuridatta held still, and feel your feet steady under you while you see that moment through.
Bhuridatta's precepts: a serpent prince who kept his precepts toward his own captor. The perfection of virtue, under pressure.
Something to keep: kept under pressure is when a precept shows what it's made of. Five of thirty.

howItsDone: In Theravada lands the Bhuridatta Jataka is told as the Bodhisatta's perfection of virtue; Mahayana teachers discuss the captain's story from the Skill in Means sutra when they talk about compassion and the precepts.

myth: every Buddhist school treats the precepts as having no exceptions at all
a Mahayana sutra tells of a captain who kills to save many, ready to bear the cost. Theravada stories like Bhuridatta's hold the line.
Bhuridatta could have destroyed the snake charmer and chose not to
the story says he shut his eyes so his anger wouldn't escape, and kept his precepts.
the captain's story says breaking a precept is fine when it's convenient
he acts to save many lives, out of compassion even for the would-be killer, and accepts the karmic cost.

fork.setup: your friend says Bhuridatta was foolish: he could have stopped the charmer and spared himself. give the strict side its best case.
options: he was scared of the spell and had no real choice.
a precept with exceptions stops being a promise; his restraint protected even his captor.
suffering is good for you, so the beating was the point.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest case for holding the line. the other side, the captain's story, answers that rules serve compassion when lives are at stake. both sides take the precepts seriously.

original.note: Pali: the naga prince of Jataka 543, who perfects virtue.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about a magic snake.
what it means: a precept kept toward the very person hurting you, and an honest debate about whether a precept should ever bend.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 543, the Bhuridatta Jataka, told as the perfection of sila; the Upayakausalya (Skill in Means) Sutra's captain story is the classic Mahayana counter-case.
guess: a serpent prince's precepts, kept toward his captor
a list of rules for snake charmers to follow
the oath a king swears on taking the throne
recall: conduct: training rules, kept as gifts

chat.says: coworker wants me to tell a customer her frame is "almost done." we haven't started. harmless, right?
options: A precept shows itself under pressure. Tell her the real date, kindly.
Harmless. A small lie that keeps a customer calm is really a kindness.
Let your coworker say it. Then it's not your lie, so it doesn't count.
chat.meaning: Bhuridatta kept his precepts even toward his captor. A coworker's nudge is a small test of the same thing.

tie.story: Bhuridatta kept his precepts even when keeping them cost him.
tie.friend: Mai can tell the customer the true date, kindly, even with a coworker nudging.

naga.meaning: a serpent being with great power in Buddhist stories

Bhuridatta.meaning: the naga prince of the Jataka who kept his precepts

Jataka.meaning: stories of the Buddha's earlier lives

Mahayana.meaning: the Buddhism of Vietnam, China, Korea, Japan and Tibet

karmic.meaning: to do with karma: an action and its results

sources.ref: Jataka 543, Bhuridatta Jataka (the naga prince keeps the uposatha precepts on an anthill; the snake charmer Alambayana seizes him with a spell; he keeps his eyes closed so his anger will not destroy the man, and keeps his virtue; made to dance in villages; freed by his family)
Upayakausalya Sutra (Skill in Means): the captain who kills a man plotting to murder the merchants aboard, out of compassion, accepting the karmic consequence

notes: Jataka 543 paraphrased; confirm the details (anthill, the charm, the closed eyes so his anger won't escape, the dancing, rescue by his family). Confirm the claim that he could have burned the man to ash.

Debate shape: Theravada Jataka (no exceptions) and the Mahayana Upayakausalya Sutra's captain (compassion may break a precept, accepting the karmic cost) each speak; neither ranked. A Mahayana scholar should confirm the captain summary; the text's number of merchants is left out.
Hard scene: the captain kills a man; told plainly in one line, without detail.
